title: Clifford Chance's Early Generative AI and Copilot Journey — The Inside View
author: Caroline Hill

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s risk-based, use-context-specific approach and materially extends it with a firmwide implementation model: long-term technical preparation, early use-case classification, environment-specific data controls, embedded restrictions, mandatory training, output verification and supervisor accountability. It offers concrete operational experience rather than measured productivity or financial outcomes.
qs: Vigneron observed: "It was important to do risk assessments and categorisations of uses cases early and the direction of the Act was reflected in our policy.

You have a personal responsibility to check the policy and output, it's how we run everything."  Lawyers have ethical and professional obligations to their clients that are core to everything they do and that is no different when it comes to Gen AI.

kp.k: Long-term technical preparation enabled rapid generative-AI deployment
kp.d: The article attributes Clifford Chance's early deployment capacity to technical foundations built before ChatGPT, including a data-science team and transformer research dating to 2018/2019. Its February 2024 global Copilot and Viva decision also followed the 2023 firmwide rollout of Clifford Chance Assist after trials involving over 1800 users.
qs: It's key to note at the outset that Clifford Chance was one of the first law firms to have a data scientist team and had been doing research on Transformers (the T in GPT) since 2018/2019, publishing its own research in 2019 1912.06905 (arxiv.org), so it had built the digital foundations required to make the most of Gen AI when it came out.

Both Microsoft and Clifford Chance itself pointed out that this February 2024 announcement followed the deployment in 2023 of Clifford Chance Assist, developed on Microsoft's Azure OpenAI platform, which was rolled out to the entire firm after trials with over 1800 users.

kp.k: The firm permitted experimentation while restricting client information
kp.d: CIO Paul Greenwood says Clifford Chance chose not to block generative AI, unlike many firms. It instead encouraged employees to experiment without client information while IT and risk teams developed controls, reflecting a belief that staff needed direct exposure to understand the technology.
qs: You've seen a lot of law firms block generative AI technology; our practice was not to do that, but to give out guidance not to use any client information but to experiment, with risk and IT working closely together behind the scenes.
We were excited from an early stage and shared the view that this was important technology that people needed to understand.

kp.k: Principles and governance preceded external AI commitments
kp.d: Greenwood and chief risk and compliance officer Bahare Heywood describe a deliberately cautious governance process: the firm took a long-term view, created a steering group, and developed firmwide principles, policy and risk-assessment processes before making external commitments. Heywood presents this work as slow and iterative but necessary for an ethical, sustainable position.
qs: We wanted to take a long-term view, and we pulled together a steering group to outline our position to clients. Our view was not to rush anything out.
One of the first things we decided before saying anything to the outside world was that we needed a set of generative AI principles, and a policy agreed across the firm.
We wanted to make sure it was sustainable, and we recognised the need for guiding principles. We felt strongly from an ethical perspective the need to make our position clear on the use of AI.
From my perspective, it was not just about policy but having a clear process around risk assessment.

kp.k: Traffic-light controls decentralised routine AI risk decisions
kp.d: Heywood says the risk framework was designed to let IT and innovation teams advance projects without returning to the risk team for every decision. The resulting traffic-light system classifies combinations of tools, data and client circumstances, encouraging low-risk experimentation while restricting uses such as reviewing CVs or personal information.
qs: Heywood's objective was to provide the IT and innovation team with the means to move forward on Gen AI projects without having to revert to the risk team in every instance, which would slow innovation down at a time when organisations such as Microsoft and OpenAI were (and still are) moving at lightning speed.
We needed a system that was easy to understand, so we brought in a traffic light system that talks about tools and types of data.
If it's green, knock yourself out. We wanted to encourage curiosity, because if you don't use and play with something, you'll never understand it. Then amber and red.
Green is certain types of tools and data that we say is fine because of where the data sits, taking into account the data, tool and client. Red might be reviewing CVs or personal information.

kp.k: Risk classification was integrated before proofs of concept
kp.d: Director of legal technology and innovation Anthony Vigneron argues that acceptable-use categories and risk assessments must precede proofs of concept; otherwise, firms will struggle to progress experiments. Clifford Chance's policy reflected the emerging direction of the EU AI Act and distinguished public ChatGPT from private Azure according to data handling and sensitivity.
qs: It was important to do risk assessments and categorisations of uses cases early and the direction of the Act was reflected in our policy.
While other firms talked about doing POCs, they hadn't done the work yet, and if you haven't done the work to agree acceptable use cases, you will find it hard to progress the POC.
We wanted to be sure we understood what was happening with the data. It's different with public ChatGPT and private Azure.
We said that there are tools where you can put in sensitive data but many were that is not the case.

kp.k: Client resistance softened through discussion of data risks
kp.d: Vigneron reports that many clients initially imposed a blanket prohibition because they feared their data would become model-training data. The article says that position subsequently reversed, while Heywood attributes resolution of disagreements to direct, informed conversations rather than treating client restrictions as fixed.
qs: The team engaged with the firm's clients on the policy and in the early stages many were worried about their data ending up as training data for the model.
They said a blanket 'no' to generative AI,
That position has now been reversed and Heywood adds: "It's about having those grown-up conversations. Where there is a disconnect, you can usually resolve it."

kp.k: Lawyers remain personally responsible for verifying AI output
kp.d: The firm's governance model keeps lawyers in the loop: users are personally responsible for consulting restrictions and checking output. Tool interfaces are intended to display relevant prohibitions at the point of use, reducing reliance on employees repeatedly consulting a separate policy document.
qs: You have a personal responsibility to check the policy and output, it's how we run everything.
Our responsibility is to ensure that the policy and guidance is clear and that when you go into a tool it's clear what the restrictions are; you don't have to go back to the policy.
When you open Teams, it will tell people 'Don't use it for x,y,and z, as those things are restricted.'

kp.k: Mandatory training extends to supervising partners
kp.d: Clifford Chance requires training on its AI policy and is teaching supervisors how the technology works. For client work, users must inform their supervisor; supervising partners must understand the relevant use and the possibility of hallucination, linking AI adoption to existing professional and supervisory responsibilities.
qs: The other thing is that we have mandatory training on the policy.
The team has also been working on training supervisors on how the technology works.
It's the responsibility of the supervising partner to understand where it is used: if you don't understand it, you can't use it.
The policy says that if you use generative AI for client work, you have to tell your supervisor.
Crucially, supervisors need to understand that this type of tool may hallucinate.

kp.k: Tool selection balanced utility, privacy, cost, and durability
kp.d: Greenwood says Clifford Chance evaluated generative-AI tools according to need, cost, data privacy, enterprise readiness, usefulness and long-term sustainability. Its Copilot decision aligned the firm with Microsoft's roadmap and reflected expectations that legal-tech vendors would increasingly integrate with Copilot rather than remain standalone.
qs: Greenwood says that Clifford Chance's decision-making process around the selection of Gen AI tools – including its GPT-4 tool Assist and property technology provider Orbital Witness – come down to cost, data privacy, enterprise readiness, and usefulness.
The first question, Greenwood says, is 'Do we need it?'

And then we look at long-term sustainability. Startups get bought. In selecting Copilot, we decided that we were going to align ourselves with the Microsoft roadmap. Microsoft has a big stake in OpenAI.
Another big part of the firm's thinking was and is that most legal tech vendors would align themselves with Copilot rather than delivering standalone products.

kp.k: Firmwide Copilot aimed to discourage alternative tool use
kp.d: Greenwood presents universal Copilot access as a risk-management benefit because employees would have less reason to use other tools. This connects enterprise deployment with governance: providing an approved general-purpose system is intended to channel experimentation into a controlled environment.
qs: According to Greenwood, one of the benefits of rolling out Copilot to everyone in the firm is that there is no reason for them to use other tools, ergo its selection saw its genesis in the early days of risk analysis.

kp.k: Current use cases augment information-intensive legal tasks
kp.d: Vigneron identifies four leading uses: summarising communications, retrieving facts from SharePoint and email, organising or originating information, and critiquing arguments. These examples describe augmentation rather than autonomous legal work, and he explicitly states that summarised output must be checked.
qs: The big use cases are summarisation, where for example, people are in a big email chain and want to summarise it to give a report to the client – all of the output will obviously need to be checked.
Or the second big one is finding the needle in the haystack. If you did a bond issue for a client and want to find out how much it was for, Copilot can search for anything in SharePoint and email.
The third one is originating information – which of the banks in this syndicate have responded? You could organise witnesses into a structure.
The fourth is creativity, where you write a document and ask Copilot what is wrong with the argument and to find the weakness.

kp.k: Internal policy retrieval demonstrates faster professional self-service
kp.d: Heywood describes a Copilot-in-Teams application that retrieves and summarises the firm's policies, identifies source material and supplies advice in four seconds, compared with a process she says can take two days. She nevertheless states that users must check the response, making the example a claimed efficiency gain subject to human verification.
qs: We have hundreds of policies and finding the right one can take two days but with Copilot in Teams, you just ask for the policy you're interested in, and it will send you a summary, where it's quoted from, and it gives me advice about it.
You'll want and need to check it, but it returns all that information within four seconds.

The other shift that Copilot will usher in is better self-service possibilities, whether that be providing staff who would have used the Clifford Chance Service Now service desk with self-service options, or enabling staff to become more self-sufficient when it comes to comes to compliance and policies.

kp.k: Practice-group monitoring feeds risks into central governance
kp.d: The legal technology team monitors use-case feedback across practice groups. Problems and risks are escalated first to practice-specific working groups and then to an overarching working group, creating a tiered feedback mechanism for governing an evolving deployment.
qs: Vigneron and his team have been monitoring feedback on use cases across various practice groups: any issues or risks have been escalated to a working group for each practice group, with that in turn fed into an overarching working group.

kp.k: Reported break-even requires fifteen weekly minutes saved
kp.d: Legal IT Insider estimates that licensing Copilot at $30 per user per month for approximately 7,000-plus employees would add $2.7m annually, while explicitly calling this rough arithmetic. Vigneron claims the system pays for itself if it saves each lawyer 15 minutes per week and says actual savings exceed that threshold, but the document provides no supporting measurement method or study data.
qs: if the firm has paid the $30 per user per month for its circa 7,000+ employees, it is adding $2.7m a year to their annual tech bill.
No doubt this is probably worse than back of a napkin math, but you get the point. It's a lot.
With Copilot if we save 15 minutes per lawyer per week it will pay for itself. And we are saving more than that.

kp.k: Comprehensive platforms may preserve future investment capacity
kp.d: Vigneron argues that investing in a tool without comprehensive coverage can exhaust available budget and force repeated requests to the CFO. This is presented as the firm's investment rationale for Copilot rather than as independently demonstrated market evidence.
qs: The difference we see in the market is that if you burn your investment firepower on something that isn't comprehensive you will have to keep going back to your CFO for another conversation.

kp.k: The guidance prioritises foundations, learning, and scalable opportunities
kp.d: The appended guidance recommends establishing policies, technical foundations, data strategy and diverse governance before deployment; aligning ambition with organisational priorities and ROI; and giving users time to learn ethics, risks, prompting, limitations, supervision and tool use. It also advocates habitual AI use, scalable everyday applications and two-to-three potentially transformative opportunities per function.
qs: Establish AI principles & policies first
Establish the right technical foundation (tech platform, data strategy)
Get your governance in place with diverse teams
Prioritise for the best ROI
Give users time to learn & explore early the new human/machine relationship with AI as the new user interface: it's important to give time and space to people to learn
AI first: to do your tasks or solve problems make it a habit to use it regularly
Identify everyday AI opportunities you can deploy at scale now
Identify two-to-three game changing AI opportunities for each function

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Vigneron describes Copilot as supporting summarisation, information retrieval, information organisation and critical review of arguments in legal work.
pts.d: Anthony Vigneron identifies uses including summarising email chains for client reports, retrieving details of earlier bond issues from SharePoint and email, identifying which syndicate banks have responded, organising witnesses, and finding weaknesses in a drafted argument. These are presented as evolving use cases that assist staff, rather than autonomous delivery of legal services. He explicitly requires checking summarisation outputs.

pts.k: Heywood reports much faster access to internal policies; Hill predicts greater staff self-service.
pts.d: Bahare Heywood contrasts potentially spending two days finding the right policy among hundreds with a tailored Copilot in Teams returning a summary, source references and advice in four seconds. This is an account of internal policy assistance, with verification still required, not a measured end-to-end saving on legal matters. Caroline Hill separately predicts better self-service for employees who would otherwise use the Service Now desk and greater self-sufficiency on compliance and policies.

pts.k: Vigneron claims that saving 15 minutes per lawyer per week makes Copilot pay for itself and that savings already exceed that threshold.
pts.d: Vigneron presents a break-even rationale for firm-wide investment and asserts that Clifford Chance is already achieving greater time savings. He also argues that investment in a comprehensive platform avoids repeated requests to the CFO for additional funding. The article does not translate these savings into verified revenue, profit, lower client fees or staffing changes.

pts.k: Greenwood expects a firm-wide Copilot offering to remove the need for other tools and anticipates legal-tech vendors aligning with Copilot.
pts.d: Hill attributes to Paul Greenwood the view that providing Copilot to everyone gives employees no reason to use other tools, linking platform selection to risk management. The article also reports the firm's expectation that most legal-tech vendors would align with Copilot instead of supplying standalone products, and Hill says this had already happened in many cases. These vendors are software suppliers, not alternative legal service providers. Selection is framed around cost, data privacy, enterprise readiness, usefulness and long-term supplier sustainability.

pts.k: Heywood and Vigneron frame advance governance and usable risk classifications as enabling faster, controlled AI adoption.
pts.d: Hill describes Heywood's objective as allowing IT and innovation teams to proceed without referring every project back to risk. Heywood reports a traffic-light system that classifies tools and data with attention to the client and where data sits. Vigneron argues that failing to agree acceptable use cases impedes proofs of concept. He distinguishes public ChatGPT from private Azure deployments and says sensitive information is suitable for some tools but not many others. These claims concern organisational adoption conditions, not a claim that generative AI is universally safe.

pts.k: The interviewees present AI use as requiring human verification, training and informed supervision, rather than removing professional responsibility.
pts.d: Greenwood stresses personal responsibility for checking both policy and output. Vigneron reports mandatory policy training. Heywood says supervising partners must understand the technology and be told when it is used for client work. Hill emphasises supervisors' need to understand hallucination risk. Tool-level restriction notices are intended to make compliant use easier. The operational model is lawyer augmentation with human oversight, not direct reliance on unverified AI output.

pts.k: The source reports that early client resistance to generative AI was reversed through engagement about data use.
pts.d: Vigneron recounts that many clients initially feared their information would become model training data and rejected generative AI outright. Hill states that this position had subsequently reversed; Heywood says conversations can usually resolve a disconnect. The account concerns the firm's client engagement and does not establish market-wide acceptance or that every client restriction disappeared.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest primarily on interviews with Clifford Chance's implementation leaders and a single-firm deployment narrative.
pts.d: Hill interviews the CIO, chief risk and compliance officer, and director of legal technology and innovation. The account supplies implementation context: transformer research since 2018/2019, research published in 2019, and a 2023 firm-wide Assist deployment following trials with more than 1,800 users. Practice-group feedback and escalation processes are described, but no performance results from them are provided. Heywood's policy-retrieval example and Vigneron's savings statement are experiential reports; no controlled comparison, time-study methodology, verification-time accounting or independently measured ROI is supplied. Hill's approximately $2.7 million annual licence-cost figure is expressly a rough estimate assuming $30 per user per month for roughly 7,000-plus employees, not a disclosed contract price. The vendor-alignment assertion is not accompanied by named examples or market data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes an early adoption journey through 2024, combining reported current benefits with undated expectations.
pts.d: The chronology runs from research in 2018/2019 to Assist deployment in 2023 and the February 2024 decision to deploy Copilot and Viva globally. The policy-retrieval and above-break-even savings statements are presented as current at interview; expanded self-service and wider vendor alignment have no fixed completion dates. Greenwood explicitly favours a long-term approach rather than rushing. Benefits and acceptable use depend on technical and data foundations, approved tool/data/client combinations, clear policies, training, informed supervisors and checking outputs. The 15-minute savings claim is a conditional break-even calculation, coupled with an assertion that the condition is already met.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate effects concern a large global law firm's lawyers, supervisors, business-services staff, clients and technology suppliers.
pts.d: Lawyers receive assistance with drafting-related tasks, summarisation and retrieval while retaining verification duties. Supervising partners must understand and oversee AI use in client matters. Employees across the firm may gain policy and service-desk self-service; risk, IT and innovation teams undertake governance, training and monitoring work. Clients are affected through use of AI in their matters and decisions about confidential-data handling. Finance leaders face a substantial platform investment justified by claimed time savings. Legal-tech vendors face the firm's anticipated shift toward Copilot integration. The source does not claim associate displacement, altered staffing leverage, lower client prices or improved access to justice.
